To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the $\mathcal Q$-parameter is a robust and useful measure of the spatial structure of a distribution of points; that, in numerical simulations of star formation, the spatial structure of the stars that form in a simulation can be quite different to the spatial structure of their natal gas; and that, in these simulations, the spatial structure and morphology of the gas does not depend on whether the simulations include feedback or not.
the stars have a spatial distribution which is substructured (or hierarchical) whereas the gas is dominated a smooth, concentrated structure.
the spatial distributions of the gas and stars in simulations of molecular cloud formation are different, despite being based on the same initial conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how does the structure of the interstellar medium (ISM) affect the spatial distribution of star formation?
the formation of stars in molecular clouds, and in particular with the spatial structure of these clouds.
the spatial distributions of the gas and stars in molecular clouds and how they are related.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gas in molecular clouds is smooth and concentrated, whereas the stars which form within the clouds are substructured.
the spatial distribution of star-forming regions in molecular clouds is hierarchical and fractal, and that this is not a consequence of feedback from stars.
, in simulations of molecular clouds with feedback, stars form with a hierarchical spatial distribution, whereas the gas has a smooth, concentrated spatial distribution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the stars are substructured, the gas is not, so it cannot be the spatial distribution of gas which drives the formation of substructure in the stars.
stars form in substructured environments, but the gas is not.
the gas in molecular clouds is smooth and concentrated, whereas the stars which form are substructured.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial structure of stars in a molecular cloud does not necessarily reflect that of the gas, and therefore the star formation rate (SFR) cannot be inferred directly from the gas structure.
the spatial distributions of the gas and stars are different, and that the gas is more smooth and concentrated than the stars.
the spatial distributions of the stars and gas in simulations are very different, and so care must be taken when comparing these two populations.
